title.narrative: Fair Finance Asia II Sida - Indonesia

description.narrative:
The Fair Finance Asia Program (FFA) envisages to reduce the negative impact of national and cross-border bank investments in Asia on human rights, the environment and climate change, and to increase adequate financial services for pro-poor, inclusive economic development. The goal is to establish a sustainable financial sector in Asia, with financial sector institutions operating at national and regional level being more transparent and accountable and adhering to Economic, Social and Governance (ESG)-criteria. FFA is funded by Sida.
This project is co-implemented by Perkumpulan Prakarsa (PRAKARSA) and Oxfam In Indonesia. Prakarsa is a local NGO working to nurture and enhance welfare ideas and initiatives through independent research and active participation for stakeholders in order to create social justice and a prosperous society. Oxfam in Indonesia has a vision of an Indonesia where people live equitably and free from the injustice of poverty, enjoy their rights, and are resilient in times of disasters. Women and girls are at the heart of all our strategies to achieve this vision. Oxfam in Indonesia has been working in 7 provinces where they support the Governmentof Indonesia, civil society, and local communities on gender justice, economic justice, and climate justice and rights in crisis.
Both organizations will be a co-lead organisation of the Fair Finance Guide Indonesia (Responsibank) coalition, and was involved in Fair Finance Guide International and Fair Financial Flows programmes.
This project aims to contribute to the FFA goals by developing the capacities of national CSOs that are also participating in the Fair Finance Guide coalition. Capacity development is undertaken to ensure that the high-level regional negotiation, advocacy and lobbyingprocess is performed by CSOs that are well-capacitated onfinancial sector issues, and are familiar and understand the financial structure in Asia. Research will be performed on 8 existing banks, with a mixture of state-owned banks and (biggest operating)banks in Asia. The research will focus its study on the role of the banks in expanding the palm oil business in Southeast Asia (as the palm oil business is held responsible for deforestation, land degradation, human rights abuse and land grabbing) and investments in cement plant and factories (as they caused social and environmental problems). As part of its influencing efforts, the financial services authority is approached to promote fair finance / sustainable finance in the country and at the regional level.
Up until now, Prakarsa as the lead organization play the major role in decision making process. Coalition member organizations are involved mostly in advocacy process with regulators. Some are involved in theresearch depends on the focus issue of the research and the expertise of organization. YLKI as consumer association played important role in financial education, TuK has focused to do campaign in the palm oil financing, WALHI is against fossil fuel financing, Kemitraan is in favor to promote climate finance, PWYP Indonesia has concern on extractive industry but not specific from the investment point of view, while other organizations at the moment do not have specific works that is directly related to financial sector.
In phase 2, there is a change in the project governance for Fair Finance in Indonesia. Oxfam in Indonesia will join the coalition andprovide an added value for strengthening the gender equality aspect, in terms of research and capacity building. Then, the project administration will need more coordination between Oxfam in Indonesia and PRAKARSA. Meanwhile, PRAKARSA is still responsible in implementing projects, providing support and oversight to execute, manage and monitor the assigned roles effectively in ResponsiBank. Onthe other hand, the members of ResponsiBank will have their own roles to assure the project activities are implemented properly based on the target plans. Role of Oxfam is to ensure the project is delivered in good quality and addressing the risk properly such assafeguarding. Oxfam is going to strengthen the element of gender justice particularly in the area of energy transition by engaging more WROs in the coalition. The activity where Oxfam in Indonesia is going to implement in this yearis conducting two times trainingon financial investment in energy sector and its impact for women.

participating-org.narrative:
We have a vision of an Indonesia where people live equitably and free from the injustice of poverty, enjoy their rights, and are resilient in times of disasters. Women and girls are at the heart of all our strategies to achieve this vision.
We have been working with local and national partners in Indonesia since 1957.
We are currently working in 7 provinces where we are support the Government of Indonesia, civil society, and local communities on the following main issues:
Gender justice: We workwith women and girls to control their body and resources, and to participate equally in all economic, social, political and cultural aspects of their lives,to have leadership roles, access to resources and services and participate in decisions that affect their lives.
Economic justice:We work through partners with marginalized small holder farmers, especially women, to adapt to climate change and improve their food security. We promote inclusive natural resource management and to promote private sector accountability which encourages respect for women-led small holders and worker’s rights.
Climate Justice and Rights in crisis: we work with communies particulalry women to be more resilience towards climate change and disaster, including in climatefinancing and mitigation that one of focus is promoting gender just energy transition. We promote risk management as everybody’s business, to strengthen and mobilize the capacity of urban areas to respond to natural disasters. We promote the mainstreaming of gender in all response intervention conducted by national andsub-national governments.

comment.narrative:
10 CSOs attended Follow the Money Training, conducted by the ResponsiBank coalition. CSOs include PRAKARSA, INDIES, Trend Asia, LBH Semarang, Indonesia CERAH, WALHI Jabar, Transparency International Indonesia, Lokataru Foundation, IGJ and Tempo Institute. There will be two more trainings this year, including one on transition finance and gender financing, which will involve organizations outside the coalition, such as those focused on advocating for women's rights.
16 organizations participated in Women in Energy convening namely: Libu Perempuan, Koalisi Perempuan Indonesia, Gema Alam West Nusa Tenggara, Yayasan PEKKA, Asosiasi LBH APIK Indonesia, Kalyanamitra, PWYP Indonesia, PPSW, PP Fatayat NU, Yayasan PIKUL, ASPPUK, Penabulu, Solidaritas Perempuan, LLHPB ‘Aisyiah, and Oxfam in Indonesia
In December 2024, a total of 20 participants attended the training on ensuring a just and equitable climate financing. The group consisted of 10 male and 10 female participants from 12 different civil society organizations (CSOs) and Women’s Rights Organizations (WRO). The training was led by two trainers: Luthfyana Kartika Larasati, Manager at Climate Policy Initiatives (CPI), and Herni Ramdlaningrum, Program Manager at PRAKARSA.
24 CSOs attended the 3 trainings organized by the ResponsiBank coalition. The CSOs came from both members an non-members of the coalition.

After the national convening, WOMANS for JET held a SHEnergy Fest, a district-level public event held in Bandung, West Java on April 27, 2025, A creative, popular, and inclusive approach was chosen to engage the audience, featuring two interactive workshops: (1) a sign language class, and (2) a zine-making workshop. Both workshops focused on the theme of women and the energy transition, providing creative and accessible spaces for learning, expression, and dialogue. This event was attended by 147 participants from WROs, DPOs, and youth groups, reflecting strong interest and growing grassroots momentum among younger and more diverse segments of the population.

comment.narrative: OJK issued the Taxonomy for Indonesian Sustainable Finance (TKBI) in February 2024, which is a transformation of the Indonesian Green Taxonomy Edition 1.0. TKBI is a classification of economic activities that support efforts and SDGs covering economic, environmental, and social aspects, focusing on the energy sector. The ResponsiBank Indonesia Coalition actively participates in providing input to OJK on the development of sustainable taxonomy in Indonesia, particularly focusing on integrating social aspects and categorizing sectors that should not be considered green, such as critical mineral mining industries (maximum categories of “transition”).

R. Joko Siswanto, the Head of Sustainable Finance Directorate, from OJK during ResponsiBank’s latest bank assessment dissemination in January 2025, mentioned that as the regulatory authority, the OJK consistently encourages broad participation from civilsociety coalitions in the development of sustainable finance. This inclusive approach is crucial, as sustainable finance serves not only to channel capital toward environmentally and socially responsible activities but also to anticipate potential risks and opportunities arising from climate change across economic sectors. To strengthen institutional coordination and policy coherence, OJK has been mandated to establish the Sustainable Finance Committee in collaboration with Bank Indonesia and the Ministry of Finance, with the aim of enhancing synergy, optimizing data systems, and developing the necessary infrastructure.

This inclusive approach is crucial, as sustainable finance serves not only to channel capital toward environmentally and socially responsible activities but also to anticipate potential risks and opportunities arising from climate change across economic sectors. To strengthen institutional coordination and policy coherence, OJK has been mandated to establish the Sustainable Finance Committee in collaboration with Bank Indonesia and the Ministry of Finance, with the aim of enhancing synergy, optimizing data systems, and developing the necessary infrastructure.

“The current definition of sustainable finance is expanded to include transitional finance to support low-carbon economies through the Sustainable Finance Law (UU P2SK). The Financial Services Authority (OJK) has also issued several regulations to createan enabling environment for sustainable finance. This includes the current update of Indonesia's green taxonomy to become the Indonesian sustainable taxonomy, focusing on the energy sector, to align the taxonomy with SDGs, social aspects, and various developments in international forums such as the ASEAN taxonomy, emphasizing fair and just transition for all. Climate change becomes a determining factor in the direction of future sustainable development, and sustainable finance needs to be a tool to achieve those goals. Collaboration among stakeholders is also crucial, including with other ministries/agencies, the private sector, academia, and civil society.” (Dian Ediana Rae, Chief Executive of Banking Supervision, OJK - delivered during a public lectureorganized by the ResponsiBank Coalition and CTSS IPB on December 12, 2023)

comment.narrative: CIMB Niaga has committed to allocating 25–26% of its total loan portfolio to sustainable financing, in line with its goal to support Indonesia’s transition to a low-carbon economy and achieve net zero emissions by 2050. This commitment prioritizes funding for emission-intensive sectors such as coal, cement, oil and gas, real estate, and palm oil that are beginning to adopt decarbonization measures. However, the bank acknowledges several challenges, including low awareness among small and medium enterprises (SMEs), perceptions that green investment is costly, and the need for incentives to encourage businesses to transition. To address these, CIMB Niaga has introduced sustainability-linked loans and incentive-based sustainable financing schemes, while also conducting public engagement initiatives like “The Cooler Earth” forum to raise awareness and foster collaboration for a more sustainable economy

BCA successfully allocated financing or credit to sustainable sectors totaling Rp 197.4 trillion. This amount of green creditconstitutes 23.5% of the total financing portfolio. Green credits as of March 2024 grew by 9.1% annually (year-on-year or yoy). BCA is offering promotional interest rates on loans to commercial debtors and SMEs engaged in environmentally conscious business activities
